quiz.q: Which of the five proofs is not a causal argument, so that Feser says the ‘What caused God?’ objection is not even prima facie relevant to it?
options: The Aristotelian proof
The Thomistic proof
The Augustinian proof
The rationalist proof
quiz.explanation: The Augustinian proof starts from the reality of abstract objects and concludes to a necessary intellect in which they exist; it does not reason from effects to a cause. The rationalist proof is tempting because it speaks of explanation, but it does argue to a necessary being as the cause of contingent things.

quiz.q: In a hierarchical causal series, what does it mean to call a cause ‘first’?
options: It is the member that came earliest in time, such as the Big Bang
It has its causal power in an underived way, and all other members borrow their power from it
It is the member nearest to the effect being explained
It is the largest and most powerful member of the series
quiz.explanation: ‘First’ means primary or underived, not temporally earliest. Even an infinitely long brush handle needs a hand with its own power. The temporal reading is the most common misunderstanding of first-cause arguments.

quiz.q: What does Stage 2 of each proof aim to establish?
options: That the universe had a beginning in time
That the cause reached in Stage 1 is the God of a particular revealed religion
That the argument’s starting point is empirically confirmed
That whatever fits the Stage 1 description must have the key divine attributes
quiz.explanation: Stage 1 reaches something fitting a key description (pure actuality, simplicity, etc.); Stage 2 derives unity, immutability, eternity, immateriality, goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience from that description. It stops short of any revealed religion.

quiz.q: A friend says: ‘Cosmologists think our universe may have branched from an eternal multiverse, so first-cause arguments are dead.’ Which response best reflects the book?
options: The four causal proofs grant a beginningless universe or multiverse for argument’s sake; they concern what sustains things in existence here and now
The multiverse hypothesis is unscientific, so it can be ignored
Only the rationalist proof survives, because it is about necessity rather than causation
Feser argues that the Big Bang proves the universe began, so the multiverse must be false
quiz.explanation: Feser repeatedly grants a beginningless universe or multiverse. The proofs are about hierarchical dependence at every moment, which a beginningless past does nothing to remove. Feser does not dismiss cosmology or argue for a beginning.

quiz.q: Why can there not be two purely actual beings?
options: Because the universe could not contain two infinite beings
Because two such beings would compete and one would defeat the other
Because distinguishing them would require a feature one has and the other lacks, which implies potentiality or parts
Because Aristotle defined God as unique
quiz.explanation: Plurality requires differentiation — a specific difference, matter, or some perfection one lacks — and any such differentiator involves parts or unactualized potential, which what is purely actual cannot have. The argument is metaphysical, not about competition or definition.

quiz.q: Which pair of claims establishes that the Unmoved Mover of chapter 1 and the One of chapter 2 are the same kind of being?
options: Whatever changes is material, and whatever is material is composite
Whatever is composite has potency (its parts only potentially compose it), and whatever has potency is composite (an actual and a potential ‘part’)
Whatever is necessary is eternal, and whatever is eternal is timeless
Whatever has intellect has will, and whatever has will is personal
quiz.explanation: The two-way entailment ‘purely actual iff simple’ is the link. The first option gives only a one-way chain about material things and does not reach pure actuality; the others concern different attributes.

quiz.q: The Thomistic proof begins from which feature of the things of our experience?
options: The real distinction between their essence and their existence
Their being composed of form and matter
Their being explicable by the laws of physics
Their beauty and order
quiz.explanation: Chapter 4 argues that what a thing is and that it is are really distinct in everything we experience. Form and matter figure in the Neo-Platonic proof as one kind of composition; order and beauty belong to design arguments Feser does not use.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think the lion/pterodactyl/unicorn example supports a real distinction between essence and existence?
options: Because unicorns are impossible, while lions are possible
Because one can fully describe what each animal is without that description revealing which exists, has existed, or never existed
Because existence is a property lions have and unicorns lack
Because the existence of animals can be known only through science
quiz.explanation: If existence were identical with essence, knowing the essence would reveal the existence; it does not. Unicorns are possible, not impossible, in the example, and Feser denies that existence is a property or accident.

quiz.q: A critic says: ‘I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does, yet they are identical; so knowing a lion’s essence without knowing its existence shows nothing.’ Which reply follows Klima, as Feser presents it?
options: Aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid are not really identical
Intentional contexts never block substitution of identicals
A complete grasp of aspirin’s chemistry would include its being acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete grasp of a lion’s essence includes its existence
Existence is merely a second-order property of concepts, as Frege held
quiz.explanation: Substitution fails only where the concepts are logically independent or incompletely grasped. The Fregean option actually states the critic’s side (Kenny’s ‘specific existence’), not the reply.

quiz.q: Which statement expresses the principle of sufficient reason as Feser defends it?
options: Everything has a cause distinct from itself
Every event is determined by prior events
Every true proposition is logically entailed by a necessary proposition
Everything is intelligible — whatever exists has an explanation of its existence and attributes
quiz.explanation: Feser’s Thomistic PSR concerns intelligibility. It is not ‘everything has a cause’ (causes must be distinct from effects), not determinism, and explicitly not the requirement that explanations entail what they explain.

quiz.q: Why can PSR say that everything has an explanation without making an exception for God, when the principle of causality cannot say that everything has a cause?
options: Because PSR is only an empirical generalization
Because a cause must be distinct from its effect, but an explanation can lie in a thing’s own nature
Because God is a proposition rather than a thing
Because PSR applies only to contingent things
quiz.explanation: Nothing can cause itself, but something can be self-explanatory. All causes are explanations; not all explanations are causes. PSR applies to everything, God included — his explanation lies in his nature.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is ‘What caused God?’ even less effective against the rationalist proof than against the others?
options: Because the rationalist proof holds that God does have an explanation — in his own nature — so there is no exception to be charged with special pleading
Because the rationalist proof concludes only to a necessary being, not to God
Because the rationalist proof admits that some things have no explanation
Because Leibniz answered the objection before Hume raised it
quiz.explanation: The rationalist proof makes no exception at all: the difference between God and the world is that one is self-explanatory and the other is not. The second option is false because Stage 2 identifies the necessary being with God.

quiz.q: Leibniz’s example of an infinite series of geometry books, each copied from the previous one, is meant to show that:
options: an infinite series of copies is impossible
books are contingent while geometry is necessary
citing each member’s immediate cause still leaves unexplained why the series exists and has the content it has
geometry must have been invented by the first copyist
quiz.explanation: The example grants the infinite series and shows that tracing immediate causes forever does not explain the whole. It is used in chapters 5 and 7 against Hume’s claim that explaining each member explains everything.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think inferring the contingency of a collection from the contingency of its members is not a fallacy of composition?
options: Because the universe is identical with each of its members
Because all part-to-whole inferences are valid
Because contingency is like weight — it adds up
Because contingency, like the redness of Lego blocks, carries over to the whole; a collection of contingent things is if anything more dependent
quiz.explanation: Whether part-to-whole reasoning is valid depends on the property. Weight does not transfer (stones), color does (Lego), and contingency behaves like color — a collection is doubly contingent. Feser does not claim all such inferences are valid.

quiz.q: What are the three versions of realism about abstract objects that the Augustinian proof considers?
options: Platonic, Aristotelian and Scholastic realism
Nominalism, conceptualism and psychologism
Direct, indirect and scientific realism
Naive, critical and structural realism
quiz.explanation: After defeating nominalism and conceptualism (the second option lists anti-realist views), Feser compares Platonic, Aristotelian and Scholastic realism and argues only the last is adequate.

quiz.q: Why is Aristotelian realism, without a divine intellect, judged inadequate in chapter 3?
options: It denies that universals exist in things
It cannot ground possibilities and necessary truths that would hold even if no material world or human minds existed
It places universals in a Platonic third realm
It treats universals as mere words
quiz.explanation: Aristotelian realism locates universals in things and in the minds that abstract them, so pure possibles (unicorns) and necessary truths that would hold without any world or human mind are left ungrounded. The other options describe Platonism or nominalism.

quiz.q: Why must the necessarily existing intellect of the Augustinian proof be purely actual?
options: Because only a purely actual being could be worshipped
Because every intellect is purely actual
Because if its existence depended on the actualization of some potential, it would exist contingently on that actualization
Because abstract objects are themselves purely actual
quiz.explanation: Necessity excludes dependence on any actualizer. That step links the Augustinian conclusion to chapter 1 and brings uniqueness, omnipotence and the other attributes. Human intellects are clearly not purely actual.

quiz.q: Patrick Grim argues that Cantor’s theorem rules out a set of all truths, and hence omniscience. Which of these is NOT among the replies Feser reports?
options: The argument proves too much, since we can truly generalize about all propositions
Omniscience requires only that there be no truth God fails to know
Divine simplicity means God’s knowledge is not a set of discrete ideas
Cantor’s theorem has been shown to be false for infinite sets
quiz.explanation: Feser reports Plantinga’s ‘proves too much’ reply, Simmons’ point that no set is needed, and Wainwright’s appeal to simplicity. He does not dispute Cantor’s theorem.

quiz.q: In Feser’s $20 illustration of proportionate causality, having the power to get genuine bills printed corresponds to having the effect in the cause:
options: formally
virtually
eminently
accidentally
quiz.explanation: A bill in the wallet is ‘formally’; money in the bank is ‘virtually’; the more fundamental power to make bills is ‘eminently’. ‘Accidentally’ is not one of the three modes.

quiz.q: How does Stage 2 of the Aristotelian proof infer that the purely actual actualizer has intellect?
options: By noting that only minds can move matter
By inferring from the order of the universe to a designer
By arguing that the ability to cause entails the ability to feel
Since it causes every possible thing, the forms of all things must exist in it (by the PPC) — not concretely but abstractly, the way forms exist in an intellect
quiz.explanation: The argument combines the PPC with the fact that the cause is immaterial: forms can exist concretely (in things) or abstractly (in minds), and only the second is possible here. It is not a design inference.

quiz.q: Cottingham objects that a sponge cake has a sponginess not present in its eggs, flour and butter. What is Feser’s main reply?
options: The PPC concerns the total cause (including the mixing and baking), not just the material ingredients, and it does not require causes to have their effects’ features formally
Sponginess is an illusion
The PPC applies only to God, not to cakes
The objection succeeds, so the PPC must be restricted
quiz.explanation: Attacking a version limited to material factors is a straw man, and the ‘heirloom’ reading ignores the virtual and eminent modes. Feser also notes the PPC is implicitly used by naturalists and respected by evolutionary explanation.

quiz.q: What does the principle agere sequitur esse state?
options: Existence precedes essence
A thing’s activity follows from and reflects what it is
Every effect resembles its cause
Being and goodness are convertible
quiz.explanation: ‘Action follows being.’ It is the formal-cause counterpart of the PPC and is used to argue for omnipotence, concurrence and against occasionalism. The first option is a slogan of existentialism, not Scholasticism.

quiz.q: Why does Feser hold that terms like ‘good’ and ‘powerful’ must be applied to God analogically?
options: Univocal use would make God a creature like us and equivocal use would say nothing; analogical use is literal yet not identical
Because all talk of God is metaphorical
Because God’s attributes are unknowable in every respect
Because only negative statements about God are true
quiz.explanation: Analogy is a literal middle ground between univocal and equivocal predication. Feser stresses that it is not metaphor and that it gives real, positive knowledge, while acknowledging much knowledge of God is negative.

quiz.q: According to Feser, Plantinga’s objection to divine simplicity misfires chiefly because it:
options: denies that God exists
reads the doctrine through a broad notion of ‘property’, a Platonist view of properties and univocal predication, all of which classical theists reject
assumes that God is material
relies on the principle of sufficient reason
quiz.explanation: Given those three assumptions, simplicity would indeed make God a property. But classical theists distinguish essence, properties, accidents and relations as constituents of things and predicate analogically. Plantinga is a theist, so the first option is wrong.

quiz.q: What is a ‘Cambridge change’, and how does it help with divine immutability?
options: A change in God’s mind prompted by prayer
A slow, gradual change too small to detect
A new description becoming true of something only because something else changed — as God becomes Creator by a change in the world, not in himself
A change that occurs only in abstract objects
quiz.explanation: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows. Likewise God’s being Creator involves real change only in the world, so God can be Creator without real change or composition.

quiz.q: An objector argues that since God causes things to exist at t1 and at t2, God must be acting at t1 and at t2, and so be in time. What is the best reply from chapter 6?
options: God acts only at the first moment of time
From ‘God causes X to exist at t1’ it does not follow that ‘at t1 God causes X’; God causes a whole temporal world in one timeless act, as an author conceives a whole story
Time is an illusion, so the problem does not arise
God is in time but unchanging
quiz.explanation: The inference confuses the time of the effect with a time of the cause’s action. Feser’s author analogy shows how a single act can produce a sequence. He does not deny the reality of time or place God in time.

quiz.q: Which analogy does Feser use to show that God’s causing and knowing all events is compatible with human free will?
options: A clockmaker winding a clock
A hypnotist directing a subject
A chess master predicting a novice’s moves
An author writing a novel in which a character freely commits a crime
quiz.explanation: The author is not a character inside the story interfering with others; the hypnotist would be exactly the wrong model, because he undermines freedom from within the story.

quiz.q: Why, on Feser’s view, does the principle of proportionate causality not imply that evil exists in God?
options: Because evil is an illusion
Because God is not the cause of everything
Because badness is a privation — an absence — rather than a positive feature that must be in the cause
Because evil is caused only by angels
quiz.explanation: The PPC concerns positive features of effects. Evil is real, but its reality is that of a lack, like blindness; making a world with evil is making good things while refraining from making others.

quiz.q: The concurrentist view of divine causality is a middle position between:
options: occasionalism and mere conservationism
pantheism and panentheism
deism and polytheism
nominalism and realism
quiz.explanation: Occasionalism denies creatures any real causal power; mere conservationism gives them power independent of God. Concurrence says creatures are real but secondary causes that act only with God’s concurrence.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say occasionalism is self-undermining for someone who accepts the proofs?
options: It contradicts the possibility of miracles
It makes God dependent on the world
By agere sequitur esse, things that truly do nothing would not truly exist — yet the proofs start from real changing, composite things, so occasionalism kicks away the ladder it climbed
It entails that God is material
quiz.explanation: Occasionalism implies only God truly exists, which contradicts both our knowledge that we exist (and are not God) and the starting points of the causal proofs. Feser’s image is climbing a ladder and then blasting it away.

quiz.q: What is Feser’s response to the thesis of ‘existential inertia’?
options: He accepts it for material things but not for souls
No composite, act-potency, essence-existence thing could tend to persist on its own, and its defenders never explain what would give it that feature
It is refuted by the second law of thermodynamics
It is true but irrelevant to the proofs
quiz.explanation: Existential inertia would let things exist without being conserved by God. Feser argues the proofs show no such thing could have this feature and that merely suggesting it ignores the arguments.

quiz.q: On the Thomistic account presented in chapter 6, a miracle is best described as:
options: an elevation of a nature beyond its own powers, or a suspension in which God refrains from conserving or concurring — not a violation of natural law
a violation of a law of nature
an event with no cause
an unusual natural event we cannot yet explain
quiz.explanation: Since laws describe the tendencies of natures, they are not ‘broken’. A resurrection adds to nature’s course; the unburnt young men in the furnace involve a subtraction. God cannot literally ‘intervene’ in his own continuous work.

quiz.q: Why does the ‘god of the gaps’ charge miss Feser’s arguments?
options: Because God is invoked only where science has already succeeded
Because Feser concedes that science will never progress
Because the proofs appeal to biological complexity
Because the proofs are strict demonstrations from starting points any empirical theory must presuppose, not probabilistic hypotheses filling a gap in current science
quiz.explanation: A gap argument allows that a non-divine explanation might be correct. These arguments claim none is possible in principle, and they start from change, composition, essence-existence and contingency — features of anything science could discover.

quiz.q: A student cites Krauss: ‘Physics shows a universe can arise from nothing.’ Which reply follows chapter 7?
options: Krauss’s physics is mathematically flawed
The universe did not arise at all but has always existed
Krauss’s ‘nothing’ — empty space with energy, or the laws of quantum physics — is not nothing, and laws cannot be ultimate explanations
Physics can never say anything about the history of the universe
quiz.explanation: Feser does not dispute Krauss’s physics; he points out that a quantum vacuum and laws are something, which Krauss himself concedes, and that laws presuppose what they govern.

quiz.q: Feser’s dilemma against scientism is that the thesis ‘only science yields genuine knowledge’ is either:
options: self-refuting (it is not itself a scientific claim) or trivial (if ‘science’ is broadened to include philosophy, in which case natural theology could qualify)
empirically confirmed or merely assumed
too narrow (excluding biology) or too broad (including astrology)
incompatible with quantum mechanics or with relativity
quiz.explanation: The scientistic claim cannot be established by scientific method, so it refutes itself; stretching ‘science’ to escape that makes the thesis vacuous and removes its force against natural theology.

quiz.q: Feser compares the argument ‘physics is predictively successful, so what physics reveals is probably all that is real’ to:
options: inferring from a metal detector’s success that only metallic things exist
a thermometer’s success at measuring heat
engineering’s success at building bridges
a map’s being smaller than its territory
quiz.explanation: A method that attends only to certain aspects of reality (the mathematically modellable) can be perfectly successful without those aspects being all there is. Feser also uses the drunk under the lamppost and the student who takes only easy classes.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think treating the most fundamental laws of nature as brute facts is incoherent?
options: Because laws of nature do not exist
Because brute facts violate the law of non-contradiction
Because physicists have already explained the fundamental laws
Because an unexplained foundation has nothing to impart, so every explanation resting on it becomes illusory — like a book on a shelf that stays up for no reason
quiz.explanation: A regress of laws is like a hierarchical series: higher laws explain only by borrowing from lower ones. Let go of the brackets in mid-air and nothing stays up. Feser also calls the move ad hoc and contrary to PSR.

quiz.q: Dawkins argues that a designer of the universe would be more complex than the universe and so need explanation. Feser’s central reply is that:
options: complexity is an illusion
the proofs agree complex things need causes, which is exactly why they conclude to an absolutely simple cause; the objection targets design arguments
God is only moderately complex
the universe is actually simple
quiz.explanation: The objection presupposes a probabilistic design argument from biological complexity. The five proofs are demonstrations, and their conclusion is divine simplicity; it is the atheist’s alternatives that are complex.

quiz.q: Why does Feser call the ‘one god further’ objection a category mistake?
options: Because Zeus and Thor might actually exist
Because atheists believe in no gods at all
Because it confuses polytheism with pantheism
Because classical theism’s God is not a member of a genus ‘gods’ but subsistent being itself — like treating triangularity as one more drawn triangle
quiz.explanation: Zeus-like gods are limited beings among beings; the God of the proofs is the source of all being and cannot belong to any genus without having parts. Feser also notes there are demonstrations for this God and none for Zeus.

quiz.q: Why does Feser think William Rowe’s evidential argument from evil (the burned fawn) poses no challenge to the book’s arguments?
options: Because animals do not really suffer

Because Rowe concludes only that God probably does not exist, and anyone with independent demonstrations of a good, omnipotent God has reason to believe a greater good is served, even if it is unknown
Because the fawn’s suffering is deserved
Because suffering is logically necessary for every good
quiz.explanation: Rowe concedes we cannot prove there is no greater good; so if the proofs succeed, we have reason to think there is one. To challenge the proofs, the evidential argument would first have to refute them.

quiz.q: According to W. Norris Clarke’s account, which Feser endorses, the ‘everything has a cause’ straw man arose mainly because:
options: Aquinas stated it in the First Way
Leibniz used it in his Monadology
Hume conflated the rationalist claim that everything has a sufficient reason with the claim that everything has an efficient cause distinct from itself
Aristotle held that God is self-caused
quiz.explanation: Descartes and Spinoza spoke loosely of God as ‘self-caused’, meaning self-explanatory. Hume read this as efficient causation, and the caricature passed through the Mills to Russell. No major defender used the premise.

quiz.q: A critic, following Kant, says the cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument. The best reply is that:
options: the ontological argument is sound after all

the necessity the proofs attribute to God is metaphysical — grounded in pure actuality, simplicity and the identity of essence and existence — not existence by definition; Aquinas rejected the ontological argument while defending cosmological ones
necessity is just a matter of linguistic convention
God exists contingently
quiz.explanation: Kant’s charge works only if ‘necessary being’ means ‘exists by definition’. Grayling’s dilemma between that and merely conditional necessity is a false one. The third option is Findlay’s objection, which chapter 6 rejects.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason, from the book, that the universe cannot be the necessary being?
options: The universe is too large to be necessary
The universe began with the Big Bang
The universe is not conscious
The universe changes, has parts and is contingent, while a necessary being must be purely actual, simple and subsistent existence itself
quiz.explanation: The reason is principled and independent of cosmology. The second option relies on a beginning the proofs never assume; the third would at best show an impersonal necessary being.

quiz.q: You are talking with a mathematician who is a convinced Platonist about numbers. Which proof is the most natural entry point?
options: The Augustinian proof
The Aristotelian proof, since mathematicians like physics
The rationalist proof, since it begins with PSR
The Thomistic proof, since numbers have essences
quiz.explanation: A Platonist already accepts realism about abstract objects — the first half of the Augustinian proof. The work is showing that abstract objects can exist only in a mind, and necessary ones only in a necessary mind.

quiz.q: What does Feser mean by calling the arguments ‘demonstrations’?
options: That they are experimentally testable
That they convince every rational hearer immediately
That their conclusions are highly probable
That their conclusions follow necessarily from premises that are certain and cannot be overturned by further empirical inquiry
quiz.explanation: A demonstration is a strict deduction, not a probabilistic or best-explanation inference. Feser explicitly denies that a demonstration must convince everyone immediately; controversy is not refutation.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that every linear causal series presupposes hierarchical ones?
options: Because things can change only if they exist, and each thing’s existence at every moment requires a concurrent series of actualizers
Because linear series cannot be infinite
Because hierarchical series always occur earlier in time
Because Aristotle’s physics required celestial movers
quiz.explanation: The coffee cannot cool unless it exists, and its existence here and now depends on a hierarchy of actualizers. Feser allows linear series to be infinite, and hierarchical series are not defined by temporal priority.
